title: Show HN: Apgar – Catch agent regressions without an LLM judge
summary: Hey HN, We build financial AI agents, and Apgar is the tool we wrote to see whether a harness change made an agent better or worse in production. Our offline evals can't cover every kind of question or session real users bring, and the LLM judge we run in Langfuse is too expensive to use on more than a small slice of traffic, so some failures get through. Apgar is a small release health checker that sits on top of our Langfuse data. It picks up the release from the production traces, and for the first hours of each new release it compares the agent's behavior with the previous release on things like tool calls per turn, retries of the same failing call, loops, output length and cost per turn (11 metrics right now). The release page shows what moved in both directions. When something gets worse, we get a Slack message (and a webhook) saying which metric moved and where the change is concentrated, for example only on Telegram or only in long sessions. We've been running it for a while and decided to open-source it: https://github.com/oimo-ai/apgar It's not meant to be another monitoring tool. We still use Langfuse for that. Apgar only tries to answer "is this release worse than the last one?" It works with Langfuse or with anything that sends OpenTelemetry. There's no LLM judge in it, so it's cheap enough to run on all traffic. The downside is that it can't tell that an answer is wrong if everything else about the turn looks the same. That's still what our evals are for. It runs on Docker Compose (or Helm) with ClickHouse, and it's Apache-2.0. The Agents page can load demo data if you want to try it without connecting anything. Curious how others deal with this. When you change your harness or prompts, how do you find out whether the agent actually got better or worse?

title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
summary:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

title: I asked my coding agent to cat a file in .ssh. It did
story_key: story|title:i asked my coding agent to cat a file in ssh it did
content_excerpt: I asked Copilot CLI whether it could read ~/.ssh . It said it had not checked and might be able to. I asked it to cat a file there. It did, with no approval prompt. ls ~ listed my home directory, also without a prompt. This was Copilot CLI 1.0.105 on macOS, a fresh directory, default settings, and a canary file in ~/.ssh in place of a real key. ~/.copilot held no saved approvals from earlier sessions. The only dialog in the whole session was the folder-trust question at startup, which says Copilot will run shell commands "with your permission" and "will remember your permissions for the rest of this session": With --sandbox it was a different program: ls ~ failed with Operation not permitted , from the sandbox, not from the model. So the sandbox works. It is off by default, and nothing in a default session tells you that. And on, its generated policy leaves outbound network open by default, as its own help text says. I went looking because of a friend. He approves every shell command his coding agent runs, one at a time, and had for months. Then Copilot updated and he stopped seeing the prompts: once he had allowed a shell command in a session, the rest went through. He looked for the sandbox boundary, could not find one, and sent me the screenshots with a one-line conclusion: "I want a sandbox the AI can play in." That is where envgit started. It is on npm now; this post is what I learned building it, including the parts that did not work. All three agents ship a local sandbox. Claude Code's is built on Anthropic's open-source sandbox-runtime (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux); Codex uses Seatbelt and Landlock; Copilot CLI's, on Microsoft's MXC, went GA this month. They are real OS-level boundaries, and envgit uses one of them underneath. But they were designed around one accident, rm -rf , and the accidents that actually cost people are different ones. The third gap is the one that matters once an agent runs unattended. A sandbox can give you back a file. It cannot give you back a push, a published package, or an issue opened on someone else's repo. Those are the actions that need a different treatment, and none of the sandboxes treat them differently. envgit is version control for the environment an agent works in. The analogy to git is literal enough to be useful: git was built for the way people change code: a few deliberate commits a day, each one a unit of intent, with the author there to write the message. title: Show HN: phpClaw – AI agent runtime for PHP with tools, memory and guards
story_key: story|title:phpclaw ai agent runtime for php with tools memory and guards
content_excerpt: Open-source AI agent framework for PHP. Tools, memory, security guards and a ReAct loop built in. Works with Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Joomla, OpenCart, PrestaShop. Any LLM provider. MIT. Tools, memory, security, and a ReAct loop, already built. Zero framework dependencies in core. Any LLM provider. One env var, one builder, one send() . The builder checks ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , then OPENAI_API_KEY , GROQ_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY , MISTRAL_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY , OLLAMA_HOST , in that order, and uses whichever it finds first. No YAML, no agent framework to learn, no vendor lock-in. An agent without tools can only talk. Register the ones your application needs and it starts doing real work: The agent decides which tools to call and in what order, running a ReAct loop (reason, act, observe, repeat) until it has an answer or hits the iteration cap. This works identically whether the tools touch your shell, your database, your HTTP APIs, or your codebase. Every "AI in PHP" tutorial ends the same way: an HTTP client bolted onto a provider API, a hand-rolled tool-call loop, and a prayer that the prompt holds up in production. A generic LLM SDK gives you the API client. phpClaw gives you the agent runtime around it: the loop, the guards, the memory, the framework wiring, already assembled. Not trying to be everything. phpClaw isn't a RAG framework: there are no embeddings or vector stores. It's built to give an LLM tools, memory and security controls against your real application, and to chain those agents into pipelines and graphs when one call isn't enough. Agent runtime. A ReAct loop with a hard iteration cap ( max_iterations , default 20), pluggable tools, pluggable memory, and skills the model loads on demand through the load_skill tool, all running inside a single reasoning cycle. Pipelines and graphs. Pipeline chains steps (prompt template, agent, structured output, your own callables) with retry and fallback. Graph runs nodes that loop, branch, pause for a human, resume in another process, and fan out to branches that run inline or are drained by workers from cron, a queue or the CLI. See Pipelines and Graphs . Provider flexibility. 7 providers auto-detected from environment variables: Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Ollama. A custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint is also supported, opt-in via PHPCLAW_PROVIDER=custom . Switch providers with ->provider() and ->model() , no code changes elsewhere. Production controls. 8

title: Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM
summary: Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.
story_key: model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0 support for mistral large 4 on vllm
content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
summary: A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images.

A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images. This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

title: Smarter cost controls for serverless
summary: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year,...
story_key: story|title:smarter cost controls for serverless
content_excerpt: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year, and thousands of customers now run mission critical notebooks, jobs, and pipelines on it. As adoption climbs, the question every platform team asks first only gets louder: how do we gain better visibility into serverless costs and keep the cost within our budget? Databricks customers running serverless SQL and Model Serving already attribute spend, govern access, and monitor consumption without touching a single cluster knob. We are now bringing that same functionality to serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and pipelines. We are making serverless cost controls work the way platform teams already expect it to. On classic compute, cost control lived in the infrastructure. You capped spend by capping machines: node counts, instance types, autoscaling ranges, and cluster policies that fenced in what users could provision. The controls were required because you had to manage the infrastructure on your own. Serverless takes those knobs away, on purpose. Provisioning, scaling, and right-sizing infrastructure is the platform's burden now, handled by Databricks, which is a big part of the value. But cost control has to live somewhere, so it moves up a layer. Instead of attaching to machines, it attaches to people and workloads. Who is allowed to run serverless, how fast a workload is allowed to spend, and where the cost lands are the questions that matter now. Classic compute answered these with three tools: tags to attribute cost, entitlements to control access, and cluster size limits to cap spend. Serverless needs the same three. Two of them exist today, and the third is coming. Attribution starts with tags. On classic compute you tagged the cluster; on serverless you tag the compute, and every DBU that compute runs carries that tag through to billing. The same table answers the audit question you will want before you change anyone's access: who is actually running serverless today, and how much are they spending? That is one more query, ranked by consumption, and the full examples live in the system tables documentation. Availability: Serverless Compute tags for attribution is currently available in Beta . Observability is already available and customers can already monitor serverless cost with system tables on AWS , Azure , and Google Cloud . title: Modeling Preference Dependencies with Directed Acyclic Graphs for Narrative-Driven Recommendation
summary: Narrative-driven recommendation allows users to express multifaceted needs through free-form text where stated preferences naturally qualify and condition one another. Existing methods typically treat narratives as flat keyword combinations or unconstrained generative queries, failing to capture how complex preferences hierarchically refine and contextualize each other. We propose the Preference Dependency Graph Framework (PDG-F), a narrative-driven recommendation framework centered on explicit preference dependencies. Specifically, PDG-A (PDG-Agent) first parses unstructured requests to organize user preferences and their mutual qualifications into a directed acyclic Preference Dependency Graph (PDG). Through this graph, candidate evidence from the open Web is acquired via directed path retrieval, and final recommendations are determined by topological path ranking. Comprehensive experiments across three diverse domains spanning English and Chinese contexts confirm that PDG-F consistently achieves superior recommendation performance over competitive baselines, open-domain retrieval agents, and frontier language models. Further diagnostic analyses show that our dependency-guided retrieval markedly raises the attainable candidate-pool ceiling, demonstrating the fundamental value of modeling preference dependencies in narrative-driven recommendation.

title: Decision Models as Judges for Hallucination Detection
summary: Large language models are widely used as judges of model outputs (LLM-as-a-Judge), but they are costly and can hallucinate or be overconfident. Decision models are a potential alternative. They return a predefined verdict with a probability for each label instead of free-form text and are much cheaper and faster. We test this promise on hallucination detection. We build binary benchmarks for five hallucination types (9,852 items from six datasets) and compare five decision models with the generative judge gpt-6-sol. Performance depends strongly on the type: the best decision model matches gpt-6-sol in balanced accuracy on context inconsistency and comes within 3 percentage points on factual errors, but trails it by 4-8 points on logical and instruction inconsistency. Decision-model probabilities are overconfident, though less so than the GPT-6 models, and separate correct from incorrect decisions only moderately. We also find that a confidence cascade of decision models improves on the best single model by 1.9-3.3 points on three types and matches or exceeds gpt-6-sol at 1-3% of its cost. Overall, decision models are a practical low-cost judge for some hallucination types but need to be validated before use.

title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. title: Game-Theoretic Solvers with Bayesian Opponent Modeling and Moral Rhetoric Framing for GLEE
summary: We describe the agent we submitted to the GLEE Competition, which plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion games against a shared pool of human and AI opponents. The agent is built around three central components: a classical game-theoretic solver to compute numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer to estimate opponent archetypes, and a language model to write accompanying messages. We utilize Rubinstein bargaining for bargaining, Faratin concession for negotiation, and Kamenica--Gentzkow disclosure for persuasion, and adapt those models to live opponents using two separate layers: a Bayesian estimate of the opponent's hidden discount factor, reservation value, or signaling reliability, and a Thompson sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings coupled with an evidence-intuition spectrum to establish message register. Most of the development effort went into the recurring problem that theoretically optimal policies perform poorly in certain live settings; we report associated failure modes, guardrails we built, and our hypotheses. We additionally evaluate our model over 13,200 Monte Carlo games against 11 synthetic opponent archetypes, an ablation of the opponent-modeling layer, and an extensive analysis of 9,337 live-game messages in which moral rhetoric framing in the persuasion setting is strongly correlated with whether the buyer purchased ($χ^2=616.7$, $p \approx 3.7\times10^{-132}$), surviving controls for quality, round, and configuration.

title: claude-code v2.1.310
summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails
